title: Acute colonic diverticulitis (adult)
subject: gastroenterology
summary: Confirm with CT when the diagnosis or severity is uncertain. Low-risk immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated disease can be managed as outpatients without routine antibiotics; give antibiotics to high-risk or complicated cases, drain abscesses larger than 3 cm, operate for peritonitis, and arrange colonoscopy after recovery when indicated.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Typical: left lower quadrant pain and tenderness, fever, leucocytosis and raised CRP. Right-sided diverticulitis is more common in Asian populations and can mimic appendicitis.

Uncomplicated: localised colonic inflammation. Complicated: abscess, perforation with purulent or faecal peritonitis, fistula (e.g. colovesical, with pneumaturia or faecaluria), obstruction or stricture.
Danger signs: generalised peritonitis, sepsis or shock, immunosuppression, inability to tolerate oral intake, uncontrolled pain.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Full blood count, CRP, creatinine and electrolytes, lactate if septic, urinalysis, and pregnancy test where relevant.

CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the imaging test of choice to confirm the diagnosis, grade severity and detect abscess or perforation. Ultrasound or MRI are alternatives (e.g. in pregnancy).
Omitting imaging may be reasonable only in a well patient with a typical recurrence of previously CT-confirmed disease; image if features are atypical, severe, or not improving.

sections.title: Uncomplicated diverticulitis
items: Immunocompetent, well, tolerating oral intake, pain controlled: manage as an outpatient with oral fluids and diet as tolerated, and simple analgesia (paracetamol).
Antibiotics are not routinely needed in low-risk uncomplicated disease (AGA 2021, ASCRS 2020, ACG 2026).

Give antibiotics if: immunocompromised, frail or significant comorbidity, systemic signs or sepsis, persistent vomiting or refractory symptoms, CRP above 140 mg/L or WBC above 15 x 10^9/L, or a fluid collection or long inflamed segment on CT.
Oral options when antibiotics are indicated: amoxicillin-clavulanate, or metronidazole plus ciprofloxacin (or levofloxacin or co-trimoxazole), usually for 4 to 7 days.
Admit if unable to take oral fluids, pain uncontrolled, significant comorbidity, immunosuppression, or failure to improve with outpatient care.

sections.title: Complicated diverticulitis
items: Admit, IV fluids, bowel rest as needed, and IV antibiotics covering gram-negative and anaerobic organisms (e.g. ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, or piperacillin-tazobactam).
Abscess larger than 3 cm in a stable patient: image-guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics. Smaller abscesses usually settle with antibiotics alone.

Diffuse peritonitis, uncontrolled sepsis, or failure of non-operative treatment: urgent sigmoid colectomy. Choose Hartmann procedure or resection with primary anastomosis (with or without diverting ileostomy) on patient stability and surgeon judgement.
Obstruction, fistula or stricture: surgical referral for resection, usually after the acute episode settles.

sections.title: After recovery
items: Colonoscopy about 6 to 8 weeks after recovery from complicated diverticulitis, and after uncomplicated disease if there are alarm features or colorectal screening is not up to date, to exclude cancer.
Elective sigmoid colectomy after uncomplicated diverticulitis is individualised (quality of life, frequency and severity of episodes, patient preference), not decided by episode count alone.
Elective resection is typically advised after a diverticular abscess treated non-operatively, and for fistula, stricture or obstruction. Use a minimally invasive approach where available.

sections.title: Prevent recurrence
items: Diet high in fibre, fruits, vegetables, whole grains and legumes, with less red and processed meat.
Nuts, seeds, corn and popcorn do not need to be avoided.
Regular physical activity, weight loss if overweight, stop smoking, moderate alcohol, and avoid regular NSAIDs unless clearly indicated.
Mesalamine, probiotics and rifaximin are not recommended to prevent recurrence.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Missing a colorectal cancer that mimics diverticulitis: arrange colonoscopy after complicated disease.
Under-treating immunocompromised patients (transplant, steroids, chemotherapy): signs are muted and perforation is more likely; lower the threshold for CT, antibiotics, admission and surgical review.
Assuming right iliac fossa pain is always appendicitis in Asian patients.
Continuing antibiotics for long courses after adequate source control.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin-clavulanate
drugs.dose: 875/125 mg orally twice daily (or 500/125 mg three times daily) for 4 to 7 days
drugs.notes: Outpatient option when antibiotics are indicated.

drugs.name: Ciprofloxacin + metronidazole
drugs.dose: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily + metronidazole 500 mg orally three times daily for 4 to 7 days
drugs.notes: Penicillin allergy. Adjust ciprofloxacin in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone + metronidazole
drugs.dose: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily + metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours
drugs.notes: Inpatient or complicated disease; switch to oral when improving.

drugs.name: Piperacillin-tazobactam
drugs.notes: Severe or healthcare-associated infection; adjust for renal function.

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 1 g orally or IV every 6 hours, maximum 4 g per day
drugs.notes: Maximum 3 g per day if under 50 kg, malnourished or with liver disease.
